title: Replies are untrusted input
objective: Produce the reply sequence that breaks a handler missing one check, or say there is none, and give the two states a dropped COMMIT leaves and the query that tells them apart.

blocks.md: A reply is input from outside your trust boundary, even when your worker sent the request it answers. Check it, and make repeating it harmless.

choice.prompt: Two copies of a reply arrive for one intent and key: `ok`, cost 80, against a hold of 100; then `ok`, cost 120. What should your handler do?

options.text: Capture 80 once; discard the second copy by key, and record its mismatch for reconciliation.
options.why: The key makes the second copy a no-op, validation keeps the bad value out, and the mismatch is evidence worth keeping.

options.text: Capture 80, then raise the capture to 120: the latest reply from the provider wins.
options.why: A cost above the hold is invalid however it arrives.

options.text: Capture both: they are two replies from the provider, so they are two charges.
options.why: One intent, one key, one effect.

blocks.md: PGlite has one connection, so deliveries cannot race here. Deliver the same valid reply twice.
blocks.direction: Script asserts: a reply captures at most once. The key row and the capture are one transaction, so a handler that raises takes its key row with it.

call.prompt: The same valid reply is delivered twice, one after the other. How many captures?

options.text: One.
options.why: The second key insert touches no row, so the handler stops before the capture.

options.text: Two.
options.why: A second delivery acts twice only if nothing durable remembers the first.

blocks.after: The key row commits with the capture, so a duplicate cannot pass the guard. Two sessions racing to insert one key under SERIALIZABLE fail differently: a unique violation for blind inserts, and a serialization failure where both checked first. The recorded race is {{run:RUN-pg-catalog}} (row H12a), and LAB-6.6's retry policy handles both.

blocks.md: If the connection drops during COMMIT, you do not know which state you are in. Run the handler again with the same key: "captured" means the first attempt did not commit, and "duplicate" means it did. The key needs no retention window.

choice.prompt: A connection drops while your handler runs COMMIT for key k1. Which states can it leave, and which query tells them apart?

options.text: The key row exists and the capture does not. Look for the capture.
options.why: That needs the key row committed on its own. Here it rolls back with the capture.

options.text: Neither exists: a dropped COMMIT always rolls back, so no query is needed.
options.why: A dropped connection hides the outcome. The commit may already have happened.

options.text: The key row and the capture both exist, or neither does. Look for the key row.
options.why: They commit in one transaction, so a commit applies both and a failed one applies neither. The key row is the evidence.

blocks.md: The rest of the handler is four more checks: the reply's status, its cost against the hold, its key, and whether the hold is still held.
A timer released the hold. Then a valid `ok` reply arrives.
blocks.direction: Model asserts: no capture after release, one capture per intent, a charge within the hold, and status ok.

code.text:
\* The handler captures on any reply that passes the checks switched on.
Handle(r) == /\ r \in inbox
             /\ captures < 2
             /\ CheckStatus => r.status = "ok"
             /\ CheckCost => r.cost <= Hold
             /\ CheckKey => r.key \notin handled
             /\ CheckLate => hst = "held"
             /\ hst' = "captured"
             /\ handled' = handled \cup {r.key}
             /\ captures' = captures + 1
             /\ last' = r
             /\ UNCHANGED <<inbox, released>>

NoCaptureAfterRelease == ~(released /\ hst = "captured")
\* Here: CheckStatus = TRUE, CheckCost = TRUE, CheckKey = FALSE, CheckLate = FALSE

call.prompt: Your handler checks status and cost only. What happens?

options.text: Nothing: the hold is already released.
options.why: A handler that never reads the hold's state captures it anyway.

options.text: The provider undoes the charge on its own.
options.why: The provider did what you asked. Undoing it is your reconciliation, not its default.

options.text: It captures a released hold.
options.why: Lateness is a check of its own, and this handler lacks it.

blocks.after: Reject the late reply, keep the release, and record a reconciliation: the provider may have charged after you gave up, and the record makes that loss visible. Drawer D-19 frames the timer as a durable obligation.

blocks.md: Your worker re-sends after a crash in CW3 and mints a new key for each attempt.
blocks.direction: Model asserts: no command is charged more than once, with a provider that honors keys.

code.text:
\* The key names the intent when FreshKey is FALSE, and the attempt when it is TRUE.
Key(c, a) == IF FreshKey THEN <<c, a>> ELSE <<c, 0>>
\* Dispatch sends [cmd |-> c, key |-> Key(c, a), att |-> a]
\* Here: Dedup = TRUE, FreshKey = TRUE, CrashWindows = {"CW3"}

call.prompt: The provider honors keys. Can the charge happen twice?

options.text: No: the provider deduplicates.
options.why: Deduplication is per key, and the second attempt carries a new one. The key must name the intent, not the attempt.

options.text: Yes.
options.why: Two keys, two effects.

blocks.after: Mint the key once, with the intent, in the command's transaction, and send it on every attempt. The [PostgreSQL 18 documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/functions-uuid.html) lists `uuidv7()`, which "Generates a version 7 (time-ordered) UUID" (read 2026-10-23). Whether PGlite supports it is part of {{run:RUN-pglite-inbound-key}}.

choice.prompt: A handler checks status, cost and key, but not lateness. Which reply sequence breaks an invariant?

options.text: An `ok` reply for cost 80 arrives twice, one copy after the other.
options.why: The key check discards the second copy.

options.text: A `declined` reply arrives while the hold is still held.
options.why: The status check rejects it.

options.text: An `ok` reply for cost 120 arrives against a hold of 100.
options.why: The cost check rejects it against the hold of 100.

options.text: The timer releases the hold, then a valid `ok` reply for cost 80 arrives.
options.why: Nothing stops the capture, so it lands on a released hold.

choice.prompt: A handler writes its key row in a separate transaction, after the capture committed. Which sequence captures twice?

options.text: The same reply arrives twice in a row, with no crash between the two deliveries.
options.why: The first delivery wrote its key row, so the second is discarded.

options.text: The capture commits, the worker crashes before writing the key row, and the reply arrives again.
options.why: The key row is missing, so the second copy passes the key check and captures again.

options.text: A reply for cost 120 arrives, against a hold that is still held.
options.why: The cost check rejects it.

blocks.title: Reading
blocks.md: The [PostgreSQL 18 documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/) (read 2026-10-23): INSERT, the ON CONFLICT clause; §9.14; §9.27.8; §13.5, Serialization Failure Handling. And Stripe's [Idempotent requests](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests), on requests that conflict "with another request that's executing concurrently" (read 2026-10-21, re-read 2026-10-23).

blocks.title: Build this
blocks.md: Write the inbound-key table and the reply validation for your handler.

RUN-pg-catalog.title: PostgreSQL 18.6 isolation catalog: rows H01-H24 in isolationtester format, the upstream baseline, the SERIALIZABLE behavior of 40001, 40P01, 23505 and 23P01, and the seeded GEN-anomaly-id grid

budget.data_directory: tmpfs, 2g (a speed choice; visibility rules do not depend on it)
budget.network: default bridge, unused during the runs
budget.step_timeout: PG_TEST_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT=10 (the tester cancels a step after 20 s and exits after 40 s); 2 for the one-permutation fallback
budget.cpu: no cap; other tasks used the host at the same time, so durations are noisy

ROW H01 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: both commit, final 20, the second debit's write returns 20 -> 20. SERIALIZABLE, only expected before, is recorded: 40001.
ROW H02 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the waiting statement updates 0 rows. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, only expected before, are recorded: 40001.
ROW H03 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the DELETE removes 0 rows and a hits = 10 row exists before and after. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H04 [agrees]: The reader's two reads total 250 at READ COMMITTED and 200 at REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE.
ROW H05 [agrees]: Both commit at READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ with a team total of -100; at SERIALIZABLE the second committer fails with 40001 and the total is 50.
ROW H06 [agrees]: Both commit at READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ (160 held against 100); at SERIALIZABLE one fails with 40001 and 80 stays held.
ROW H07 [agrees]: Run from the upstream specs: REPEATABLE READ gives s3 a state no serial order shows; SERIALIZABLE aborts s2 with 40001 (-2); DEFERRABLE makes s3 wait (-3).
ROW H08 [agrees]: 6 of 210 permutations fail with s3 READ ONLY; the READ WRITE variant is measured here, not read from the spec comment.
ROW H09 [agrees]: The second count is 3 at READ COMMITTED, 2 at REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE.
ROW H10 [agrees]: With one session SERIALIZABLE and the other READ COMMITTED both commit, in both assignments and both commit orders; with both SERIALIZABLE one fails with 40001.
ROW H11 [agrees]: A sequential scan aborts a SERIALIZABLE transaction that shares no row with the other; the same transactions on an index scan over distant keys both commit.

ROW H12 [agrees, with additions]: 23505 and 23P01 appear under SERIALIZABLE; which of 40001 and 23505 appears depends on whether the failing session checked first and on the order, and a whole-command retry with a re-check ends without error where a blind retry fails again.
ROW H13 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the statement waits, then updates the row it could not see. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H14 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: 23505, no restart. REPEATABLE READ: 23505. SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H15 [agrees]: Disjoint claims at all three levels; the count through SKIP LOCKED is 0 while 4 jobs are pending.
ROW H16 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED returns the rows out of order; REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE raise 40001; FOR UPDATE in a subquery returns them in order.
ROW H17 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: mallory sees 'secret from mallory'. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: her locking read fails with 40001, so it is prevented by failure.
ROW H18 [agrees]: CHECK accepts NULL, the guarded UPDATE skips the NULL row, USING hides it, WITH CHECK raises 42501; the same at all three levels.
ROW H19 [agrees]: 22003 'bigint out of range' at all three levels; the balance is unchanged; sum(bigint) is numeric.
ROW H20 [agrees]: Row 1 is never delivered: the mark is 2, both ids exist, the next poll returns nothing; the same at all three levels.
ROW H21 [agrees]: Both permutations of the regression test end with bar's 40001, the output the upstream file expects.

ROW H22 [differs]: Ascending order removes the deadlock and both commit at READ COMMITTED. At REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, 4 of the 6 ascending-order permutations still fail with 40001 (first updater wins), so ordering is no substitute for the retry.
ROW H23 [agrees]: B's COMMIT fails with 40001; its retry reads 20 available, the guard refuses (0 rows) and nothing is written.
ROW H24 [agrees]: REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: B fails with 40001 and its retry updates 0 rows. READ COMMITTED: no error, 0 rows.
notes: The tester is PostgreSQL's own isolationtester, built from the 18.6 source tarball and run against the Debian-packaged 18.6 server of the postgres:18 image; it is not statespace isorun (W4-T16).

isolationtester prints errors as 'ERROR:  <message>' without a SQLSTATE. SQLSTATEs come from the server's csv log: each session's application_name is '<tag>/<session>', and for every session the messages the tester printed must equal the messages the server logged, in order; a mismatch stops the run.
NULL prints as an empty cell in isolationtester output; an empty string prints the same way.

A session that continues after an error meets 'current transaction is aborted' (25P02) at its next write. Those follow-on errors stay in the row outputs, as after_abort in the index, and keep a history out of the GEN-anomaly-id pool.
The lock model that decides which interleavings cannot hang the tester is sound and incomplete; every lock wait the tester reported was one the model predicted.
The grid's 'half' split, the target counts and the retry patterns are design defaults [D], not measurements.
Nothing was emulated: no browser, phone, hosted service or other PostgreSQL version was involved. PGlite is a different instrument (W0-S08).
